title: Perplexity Time Machine API Launches Point-in-Time Search
summary: Perplexity's Time Machine API adds point-in-time web search to Search and Context APIs. 365-day historical window, $5 per 1,000 requests, no archive premium.
body_markdown:
#### 💡 TL;DR


- Perplexity launched Time Machine API on November 25, 2026, adding point-in-time web search with a 365-day historical window for Search and Context APIs.
- The snapshot_as_of parameter returns pages as they existed at a chosen past date, priced at $5 per 1,000 Search requests and $1 per 1,000 Context URL fetches.
- Perplexity reports Time Machine cut zero-gradient training groups from ~90% to ~25% on forecasting evaluations using GLM-5.3 Flash and Polymarket questions.


Perplexity shipped Time Machine for its Search and Context APIs on November 25, 2026, enabling developers to retrieve web pages as they existed at a chosen past date. The new snapshot_as_of parameter reaches back 365 days, letting teams run queries against historical copies rather than the live web. Pricing remains $5 per 1,000 Search API requests and $1 per 1,000 Context API URL fetches, with no surcharge for historical access.


The launch targets evaluation workflows where later information distorts results. Forecasting models, reinforcement learning pipelines, finance backtests, and compliance audits require fixed evidence sets that exclude future outcomes. Perplexity's internal training work with GLM-5.3 Flash showed that answer leakage reduced useful learning signal by roughly two-thirds: about 90% of training groups had zero gradient with live-web access, dropping to about 25% when Time Machine enforced temporal boundaries.


## How the Archive Works


Perplexity's crawler stores a dated copy each time it visits a page, creating a sequence of versions tagged with capture timestamps. When a Search API request includes snapshot_as_of, the system filters candidates to pages published or first crawled by that cutoff, then swaps each with its newest archived version no later than the specified date. Ranking, title extraction, and snippet generation operate on the older text. The Context API applies the same logic for full-text reads, ensuring search and retrieval share a single historical view.


The timestamp must follow RFC 3339 format with a time zone. Future cutoffs and requests outside the 365-day window are rejected. Domain and language filters remain available, but search_recency_filter, publication-date and last-updated filters, and People Search do not work with the cutoff. Historical responses omit the last_updated field, and pages unavailable at the specified time are dropped. A query may return fewer results than max_results, or none.


## Context API Historical Reads


Historical Context API requests never fetch live pages. For successful reads, metadata.origin is cached, and metadata.fetched_at records when the copy was obtained. Markdown, query highlights, and yes/no criteria scoring are available, while HTML and links are not. A URL returns no_content when no copy exists at or before the cutoff, when the page returned 404 or 410 then, or when the stored copy is unreadable. The cutoff cannot be combined with max_age_seconds, cache_only, or if_modified_since controls.


## Reinforcement Learning Use Case


Perplexity trained GLM-5.3 Flash on resolved 2026 political questions from Polymarket, limiting search to information available when each question was asked. Before training, the model scored 0.94 on held-out questions with live-web access versus 0.77 with Time Machine; the Polymarket price on the question date scored 0.79. After training with Time Machine, the model's held-out reward rose to 0.80, above the market score. The contrast showed how outcome lookups produce identical forecasts and collapse learning signal: about 90% of live-web training groups had zero gradient, versus about 25% with Time Machine.


## Accuracy Benchmarks


Perplexity compared Time Machine to Exa Snapshot across three sets of 1,000 queries: random, news, and prediction-market research. Time Machine returned publication dates on 98.8% to 99.5% of pages, compared with 66.1% to 77.7% for Exa. An automated judge flagged pages containing information from after each cutoff. The largest gap appeared in the random sample: 0.25% of Time Machine pages were flagged versus 1.10% of Exa pages, and 18 Time Machine queries versus 62 Exa queries returned at least one flagged page. Gaps were smaller for news and prediction-market queries.


## Release Date and Pricing


Officially launched on November 25, 2026, Time Machine is available to existing Perplexity API customers with no new endpoint or setup. Teams can add the cutoff parameter to current workflows. The default rate limit applies, and customers seeking higher limits can contact Perplexity's API team. Beyond forecasting, use cases include finance backtests with cutoffs hours before earnings calls or FOMC announcements, compliance audits of pricing pages and terms of service at two timestamps, and agent replay for debugging.


## What This Means


Time Machine transforms retrieval APIs into temporal infrastructure. Developers gain a common layer for live queries, historical evaluation, and audit trails without maintaining separate archives. For reinforcement learning, the temporal boundary prevents answer leakage and restores training signal. For finance and compliance, point-in-time reads anchor analysis to the information set available when decisions were made. The 365-day window and zero-surcharge pricing make temporal search a default capability rather than a specialized add-on, shifting archive coverage from an operational burden to a standard product feature.
